title: Finding a dermatologist who knows dark skin
question_forms: How do I find a dermatologist who knows dark skin?
Do I need a Black dermatologist?
What should I ask a dermatologist about dark skin?
tradition_says: Many Black people have been told they were seen by someone who had never learned to read their skin, and pass on the names of doctors who do.

layer1.plain_answer: Dark skin is under-represented in textbooks, and in one test dermatologists and AI both did worse on dark-skin photos, so it is fair to ask a clinician about their experience. In the UK a GP referral is the route; the BAD hub shows how common conditions look on black and brown skin.

do.text: Ask your doctor for a referral if treatment is not helping; the UK's NHS may refer you to a dermatologist.
Read the BAD hub on how common conditions look on black and brown skin before the appointment.

source.name: British Association of Dermatologists, Patient Hub, "Skin of Colour"

do.text: Ask what share of their patients have skin of colour and where they trained for it.

source.name: Black Health (blackhealth.org), "How to find a Black dermatologist", updated Sep 2026

do.text: Photograph the area in bright natural light on a neutral background and take close-ups.

source.name: Black Health (blackhealth.org), "How to find a Black dermatologist", updated Sep 2026

avoid.text: Assuming a specialist will recognise your condition from a textbook picture: the dark-skin share of images in medical textbooks is small.
Treating a US directory as a UK guide: the Black Health article is about US clinics and insurance.

source.name: Black Health (blackhealth.org), "How to find a Black dermatologist", updated Sep 2026

see_someone_when: A skin problem is not improving with treatment (doctor).
A mole or mark is changing (doctor, soon).
You were told "it is nothing" and the area is still changing (ask for a second opinion).

tested.population: 656 skin images (207 Fitzpatrick V-VI) in the Diverse Dermatology Images dataset; dermatologists and AI
tested.design: Test of AI models and dermatologists on skin images by skin tone
tested.finding: AI models did worse on Fitzpatrick V-VI than I-II (for example ROC-AUC 0.55 against 0.64 for ModelDerm, with overlapping 95% intervals of 0.46 to 0.64 and 0.55 to 0.70; DeepDerm 0.50 against 0.61, HAM10000 0.57 against 0.72; figures from the full text, PMC9374341, opened 12 Nov 2026); dermatologists were also worse on dark skin; fine-tuning on the dataset closed the AI gap.

source.authors: Daneshjou R, Vodrahalli K, Novoa RA et al

tested.note: From the research file (full text read 12 Nov 2026). Photos, not live clinic visits.

tested.population: 4,146 images from four core US medical textbooks
tested.finding: 74.5% of images showed light skin, 21% medium and 4.5% dark.
tested.note: General medical textbooks, not dermatology texts.

tier_driver: That clinicians and algorithms do worse on dark-skin photos and that teaching images are mostly light-skinned: one image-based experiment and one audit. Whether seeing a dermatologist with dark-skin training improves outcomes is untested.
tier_note: Observational image studies; no patient-outcome study. Directory advice comes from a US advocacy-style source and is labelled common advice.
harm_note: The harm is a missed or late diagnosis.
evidence_summary: In an experiment with 656 photos, 207 in Fitzpatrick V-VI, an AI model performed worse on dark skin and dermatologists did too. Medical textbooks showed 4.5% dark skin in one audit. The Black Health article lists directories and questions to ask, with a US focus. For UK use, the GP route and the BAD hub are the opened sources; I did not find a UK directory by skin of colour.
gaps: Untested: whether seeing a dark-skin-experienced dermatologist improves outcomes; no UK directory of dermatologists by experience with skin of colour was found. The Black & Brown Skin handbook (blackandbrownskin.co.uk) loaded but showed only a tagline and a link to the handbook; its contents were not read, so it is named here but not cited as evidence.

sources.name: British Association of Dermatologists, Patient Hub, "Skin of Colour"
